turn_text: So the methane fee has been another provision that has caused some consternation among some of your colleagues. Do you see it surviving at this point?

Well, we're still battling over the methane fee. Obviously, methane is 80 times more powerful than traditional greenhouse gases. And so we're working very hard to make sure we have a provision in the final bill that incentivizes dramatic and quick. reductions of methane into the atmosphere. And I'm still very optimistic that we will be able to reach an agreement that maybe doesn't have everything that I would want, but it still is substantial and will help us to meet the goal. And the important thing is that methane is important in the short term. It's life expectancy is not as high as traditional greenhouse gases. So looking at 2030, the more that we can reduce methane, the more likely we're going to reach the high goals that we've set for our country.

turn_text: So no one knows better than you do how hard it is to get climate policy through Congress. What do you think has changed since Waxman-Markey died what a decade ago? What's changed since then?

That's something that we did not have 10 years ago. We now have an army of activists, the sunrise movement, youth strikers who are out in force. And right now, finally, we only need 51 votes. Back in 2009, we needed 60 votes because we're using reconciliation.
